title: Palantir, Microsoft’s biggest warning gets real for AI stocks
excerpt: A long-running AI concern is becoming harder to ignore
content_html:
In July, Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella surprised AI stock investors with an uncomfortable way to think about what they were buying into.

As I wrote for TheStreet in "Microsoft CEO adds fuel to Palantir CEO's AI warning," Nadella argued that companies weren't merely paying for tokens. Moreover, they were feeding outside models the prompts, corrections, and institutional knowledge that eventually make those systems useful for their users.

"You essentially pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable," Nadella wrote in his July essay.

Days later, that warning became a central part of Palantir's bull case. Now, two months on, Palantir and Nvidia, two of the biggest names in the AI space, are starting to act on it.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp pushed the argument further, which I covered in "Palantir CEO escalates Microsoft's AI warning."

During the company's August earnings call, Karp warned businesses that they could potentially end up aiding an outside AI provider build "a competitive business that doesn't require your business or your people."

That sovereign-AI thesis has become a critical part of Palantir's bull case, alongside powerful commercial growth that has driven the stock up around 51% in August alone, as Jim Cramer recently explained.

That said, the debate's now moving beyond speeches. Reuters reports that Palantir and Nvidia are now taking concrete steps around how frontier AI models interact with sensitive corporate information.

Palantir is drawing a harder line on AI data control

The Palantir-Anthropic tension is becoming a lot less about abstract AI safety and more about who gets to keep data, for how long, and under what terms.

Reuters, citing The Information, says Palantir pressed Anthropic for an irrevocable zero-data-retention guarantee before allowing Anthropic models to be made accessible through Palantir's software. 

Clearly, Palantir is looking for contractual certainty that sensitive prompts usage data and outputs cannot later be retained, repurposed, or exposed through policy changes.

The dispute between the two businesses has intensified after Anthropic switched up the policy for its Fable model in June, which allowed companies to retain usage logs for 30 days to defend it against attacks.

That change led to a customer pushback. At the same time, OpenAI faced similar scrutiny over allegations that user data could potentially be used in model-related work, according to the report.
